children: 0358 GMT - The U.S. dollar will be the key factor in how gold prices perform over the coming months, according to Commonwealth Bank of Australia analyst Vivek Dhar. "Structural safe-haven demand has moved further into the background as the 'Sell America' and 'U.S. dollar debasement' trade has given way to traditional market relationships like the inverse relationship between gold and the U.S. dollar, and gold and U.S. 10-year real yields," Dhar says. The U.S. dollar has already risen quicker than CBA anticipated, and is just shy of a peak the bank was predicting for mid-2027. "This suggests limited downside risks to current gold prices," says Dhar. CBA expects gold to end the year around $3,500-$3,700/oz. Spot gold is down 0.1% at $3,580.89/oz. (rhiannon.hoyle@wsj.com; @RhiannonHoyle)

0341 GMT - Australian private-sector business investment surged 12% on quarter in 3Q, the largest quarterly gain since a 2011 mining boom and far above the 4.3% consensus. The surge was driven by a 23% jump in equipment, plant and machinery investment from AI-related spending. Josh Williamson, chief economist at Citi, says domestic demand could accelerate by up to 1.5% in 3Q, taking yearly growth to a "too hot" 3.3%. With demand running above potential and the AI boom competing for land, labor and capital, Williamson sees the RBA holding the official cash rate at 4.85%, with upward risk of another hike. (james.glynn@wsj.com; Twitter @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0318 GMT - Asian currencies will continue to tread water as a fresh U.S. tariff salvo rekindles trade uncertainty, Maybank analysts say. Fracturing trade relations are negative for the dollar and the DXY index has fallen since the tariffs were first brought to attention, they write. The Trump administration has proposed duties targeting 14 economies over excess manufacturing capacity. Vietnam faces the highest proposed rate, followed by India, and then China and Singapore. Maybank notes that product exemptions--particularly for semiconductors and pharmaceuticals--could cushion the impact on Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore and Malaysia. There is also scope for negotiations to yield lower potential rates. With hearings scheduled to start in late January, tariff-related uncertainty could persist well into 1Q 2027, Maybank says. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0308 GMT - Australians are nervous about the risk of a coming recession, given that inflation remains elevated despite rising unemployment. Still, the alarm might be misplaced, says Jonathan Kearns, chief economist Challenger. Australia is more likely to have a recession when other countries like the U.S. are also in recession, he says. Economic models indicate the probability of a recession in the U.S. is just over 10%, he adds. The same models suggest the likelihood of a recession in Australia is low. But with the Reserve Bank of Australia needing to keep policy tight for some time to squash high inflation, there is always the risk it squeezes too hard, he adds. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0224 GMT - Bitcoin pops back above the closely watched $60,000 mark in early trade, in line with a rebound in tech and AI stocks. The cryptocurrency has been moving in tandem with the equities selloff as both are sensitive to risk appetite and interest-rate expectations. Bitcoin's morning gains follow a drop overnight after U.S. inflation data firmed up Fed rate-hike bets, suggesting that dip-buying could be kicking in. Still, the outlook remains fragile. Tighter global financial conditions and the likelihood of more selloffs fueled by concerns about the sustainability of the AI trade suggest that a lasting rebound in crypto will be challenging. Bitcoin rises 1.1% to $60,889, but stays stuck at four-month lows. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0146 GMT - Long-term Japanese government bond yields are higher as sharp gains in semiconductor and artificial intelligence-related stocks hurt demand for government bonds as safe-haven assets. Stronger-than-expected 3Q U.S. GDP and elevated U.S. inflation data keep expectations intact for further rate increases by the Federal Reserve. That in turn could raise the prospects of the Bank of Japan's continued tightening. Earlier Thursday, BOJ board member Naoki Tamura said the central bank should bring its policy rate to neutral levels soon, as financial conditions are still accommodative. The 10-year JGB yield is up 1.5 basis points at 2.660% and the 5-year yield is 3.5 basis points higher at 2.080%. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

0146 GMT - The Indian rupee looks set for further gains into 2027 as lower crude prices reduce oil importers' demand for dollars, OCBC FX strategist Sim Moh Siong says in a note. Improving equity inflows as investors rotate away from artificial-intelligence-heavy markets will also add to the rupee's gains, Sim says. The Reserve Bank of India is likely to use periods of rupee strength to rebuild foreign-exchange reserves, which should temper the pace of appreciation. OCBC forecasts the dollar at 92.10 rupees by the end of 2027. The rupee closed 0.7% higher at 92.23 against the dollar on Wednesday, according to LSEG data.(venkat.pr@wsj.com)

0136 GMT - Asian currencies consolidate against the dollar in early trade, but may be weighed by risk-off sentiment. Mounting doubts over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade rattled Wall Street for a second straight day on Wednesday, UOB's Global Economics & Markets Research team says in a note. Investors are navigating concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom, rising borrowing costs and renewed tariff risks, Commerzbank Research analysts say in a note.The U.S. dollar is little changed at 159.09 yen and flat at 1.2901 Singapore dollars, while the Australian dollar is 0.2% higher at US$0.6638, according to LSEG data.(amanda.lee@wsj.com)President Emmanuel Macron has suggested a "golden rule" to balance the budget, ING's Chris Turner says. "Euro Could Stay Weak Against Dollar For Now — Market Talk," at 0841 GMT Wednesday, misspelled President Macron's name.

0121 GMT - There are good reasons to think the Bank of Korea's tightening cycle is either nearing its end or already over, Capital Economics says after the central bank delivered its third rate hike of the year. The BOK's main concern is inflation, which has remained above its 2% target since the conflict in Iran began, says economist Gareth Leather. As base effects from the energy shock fade, Leather expects inflation to fall back toward the target early next year. Growth has also been concentrated in capital-intensive sectors and strong increases in productivity have helped prevent rapid GDP expansion from generating significant domestic price pressures. The won's strong rebound will also help ease concerns about imported inflation. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0120 GMT - The risk-reward of chasing dollar gains looks less attractive, but the prospect of a more hawkish Fed should keep the greenback supported, OCBC FX strategist Sim Moh Siong says in a note. The dollar's relation with stocks could remain choppy, caught between safe-haven demand and concerns that a deeper artificial-intelligence slowdown could weigh on U.S. growth, Sim says. A December Fed rate-hike is priced in on strong growth and sticky inflation, but a 50 bps move looks unlikely as the stock selloff has already tightened financial conditions, the strategist says. The ICE U.S. Dollar Index is up 0.1% at 103.73, according to LSEG data. (venkat.pr@wsj.com)

0016 GMT - Japanese stocks are higher, rebounding from Wednesday's sharp declines, thanks partly to signs of U.S. economic strength. Semiconductor and metals stocks are leading the gains. Kioxia Holdings is up 11%, SoftBank Group is up 5.3%, and Sumitomo Metal Mining is 4.9% higher. The dollar is at 159.11 yen, compared with Y159.38 as of Wednesday's Tokyo stock market close. Investors are focusing on crude oil prices and bond yields. The Nikkei Stock Average is up 1.3% at 57745.27. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)
